title: Maximum demand: what the whole building draws

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the neutral bar fall from 24.35 A to 0.30 A as the three phase bars even out, when you drag DBL2's circuits off L1 and share them across L1, L2 and L3.
interactive.title: What the whole building draws
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A refresher lesson in twelve screens, with Back and Continue between them, on maximum demand: what the whole building draws, how it is shared across the three phases, and diversity. Screen 1, Do you still have it?: "Your slides give a diversity percentage for a lighting circuit. Is diversity a rule you must apply?" Three choices, in this order: "Yes: BS 7671 sets the percentages"; "No: it is guidance, used where common sense allows"; "Yes, wherever the On-Site Guide gives a percentage". Right: "Still there.", with your slides p.10: the percentages are only found in the On-Site Guide, so they are guidance and do not have to be applied,[^1] and ten 100 W lamps could be designed at 660 W rather than 1000 W;[^2] then the two slips in a line each, and two buttons: Refresh the why (on to screen 2) and Skip to the practice (straight to screen 7). Wrong, the first: BS 7671 itself has no diversity table; Regulation 311.1 has the designer assess maximum demand and lets diversity be taken into account, and the On-Site Guide gives the recognised figures.[^3] Wrong, the third: even where it gives one, it may be left off: 66% for a domestic lighting circuit[^4] and 90% for a shop's lighting[^5] are On-Site Guide figures, applied only where the loads really do not all run together.[^1] Then the right answer and on to screen 2, with no skip. Read: diversity is guidance, not a rule (slides p.10). Screen 2, What it is for: maximum demand is the largest current an installation draws at any one time.[^6] The supply and each submain are sized from it: Regulation 311.1 accepts it may be worked out for the whole installation or a part of it,[^7] so each board gets its own figure. Your assignment asks for it in question 10, "making informed assumptions where necessary",[^8] linked to question 1b's balancing.[^9][^10] In red, if it is skipped or wrong: too low, the supply fuse, or a submain's device and cable, carries more than it was chosen for (the course's reasoning); too high, the cables are bigger and dearer than they need be.[^11] One line: a figure with diversity is an estimate, which the IET accepts may occasionally be exceeded.[^12] Screen 3, The why: the opening text says each of DBL2's lighting circuits runs between one line and the neutral; equal currents on L1, L2 and L3 cancel in the neutral, as your slides say of a balanced three-phase load (p.33),[^13] but unequal ones do not,[^14] so the neutral carries the imbalance; and the heaviest phase sets what the supply must carry.[^15] The picture: three columns, L1, L2 and L3, each holding the circuit cards on it, and four bars on one scale that fits 24.35 A: L1, L2, L3 and N, each with its current. Seven cards, the course's own circuits for DBL2 (screen 8 gives what each feeds), each with a short name and its current: C1 Consultation 4.89 A; C2 Toilets W 4.08 A; C3 Toilets E and tea 5.71 A; C4 Stores 2.63 A; C5 Showroom E 3.33 A; C6 Reception 2.50 A; C7 Foyer 1.21 A. It opens with all seven on L1: L1 24.35 A, N 24.35 A. "Drag a card to another phase, or tap it to move it on." Two buttons: All on L1, and The course's split (L1: C1 and C5, 8.22 A; L2: C3 and C6, 8.21 A; L3: C2, C4 and C7, 7.92 A; N 0.30 A). Two readouts: Heaviest phase (its label names the phase), and Neutral. Under them the rule: for currents at about the same power factor, IN = √(I1² + I2² + I3² − I1·I2 − I2·I3 − I3·I1), the sum of three currents a third of a cycle apart (the AC circuits course); under it, mains-frequency currents only: fluorescent and LED fittings also draw third-harmonic currents, which add in the neutral instead of cancelling (lesson 4). One line: the card currents rest on practice values (screen 6). Read: with all seven on L1 the neutral carries 24.35 A, as much as L1; shared as the course shares them it carries 0.30 A, harmonics aside, and the heaviest phase is 8.22 A. Screen 4, Check: "A board's lighting circuits carry 10 A on L1, 10 A on L2 and 4 A on L3, at about the same power factor. What does the neutral carry?" Choices 24.00 A (added as if on one line: they are a third of a cycle apart, so they partly cancel), 6.00 A (right) and 0.00 A (only equal currents cancel), and a Why?: the 4 A on each phase cancels, leaving 6 A on L1 and 6 A on L2, whose sum is 6 A; by the rule, √(100 + 100 + 16 − 100 − 40 − 40) = √36 = 6.00 A. Read: the neutral carries 6.00 A. Screen 5, Diversity, as common sense: not every load runs flat out at once, so a building draws less than its connected load; your slides call diversity designing with common sense rather than the maximum.[^16] The allowances this lesson uses, from the On-Site Guide's column for small shops, stores, offices and business premises (the course reads a showroom into it, its own assumption; a training provider warns that commercial work may need measured loads instead[^17]): lighting 90% of the total current demand;[^5] heating and power 100% of the largest appliance plus 75% of the rest;[^18] motors 100% of the largest, 80% of the second largest and 60% of the rest (the showroom has only one);[^19] standard circuits 100% of the largest circuit plus 50% of every other.[^20] Only these; read the rest in your copy. EV charge points: the IEC wording sets the factor at 1 unless a load management system is used;[^21] Regulation 722.311 lets load curtailment count,[^22] and your guide makes load management optional.[^23] In a fold, Where it's argued: on the IET forum one contributor says BS 7671 does not prohibit diversity on EV points,[^24] another that without load management it is still none;[^25] your slides apply 66% to one lighting circuit's Ib,[^2] a training provider applies diversity only to the total at the origin,[^26] an IET answer says it might only rarely be appropriate for one circuit,[^27] and the Schneider guide applies its factor to the loads on a board[^28] and advises close to 1 for mainly lighting.[^29] Then the course's choice: the lighting at 100%, because question 5a has the showroom lights on together from 7.30 am to 9 pm (pack p.4); the On-Site Guide would allow 90%, a designer's call. Screen 6, Worked example, a line at each press: your slides' circuit (p.10), 10 × 100 = 1000 W; 1000 × 0.66 = 660 W;[^2] Ib 660 ÷ 230 = 2.87 A against 1000 ÷ 230 = 4.35 A, the smaller cable your slides mean.[^11] Then one 4 × 36 W modular fitting from the drawing's key:[^30] 4 × 36 = 144 W of tubes; tube watts leave out the ballast,[^31] and 25% may be allowed when no loss is given,[^32] so 144 × 1.25 = 180 W; at 0.96, an electronic ballast's power factor,[^33] 180 ÷ (230 × 0.96) = 180 ÷ 220.8 = 0.82 A. One 26 W LED fitting:[^34] at 0.95, as a maker states for a similar panel[^35] (another states 0.97[^36]), 26 ÷ (230 × 0.95) = 26 ÷ 218.5 = 0.12 A. Labelled: 25%, 0.96 and 0.95 are practice values, since the drawing does not name the fittings' gear; read the real ones from the maker, whose watts for a separate driver are extra.[^37] One line: an older book instead takes lamp watts × 1.8 ÷ voltage for discharge lighting at a power factor of at least 0.85;[^38][^39] the course uses the first method. Screen 7, Section A, the course's question 3 (a): the showroom's scenario panel, from your assignment (pack p.3 and 4),[^40][^41] and the course's split, said as its own: DBL2, in the tools and warranty store, feeds the east of the building (the consultation bay, the toilets, cleaner and tea bay, the two stores, the showroom east of the welcome desk, service reception, the foyer and the walkway bollards); DBL1 the rest. Counted on your lighting drawing, DBL2's share: 55 LED 26 W, 18 modular 4 × 36 W, 4 twin 58 W and 6 walkway bollards 18 W.[^34][^30][^42][^43] The key does not say whether a twin's 58 W is each tube or the fitting: the course takes two 58 W tubes, 116 W, the cautious reading. "(a) Determine the connected lighting load of DBL2, from the key's wattages." A typed answer (part 3a, in W, whole watts): 55 × 26 = 1430 W; 18 × 144 = 2592 W; 4 × 116 = 464 W; 6 × 18 = 108 W; 4594 W. Slips: 2650 W (each modular fitting as 36 W: it holds four tubes), 4486 W (the bollards left out), 4362 W (the twin as 58 W in all: the other reading; the course takes two tubes). Read: DBL2's connected lighting load is 4594 W. Screen 8, Section A, the course's question 3 (b): (a) carried forward at 4594 W. DBL2's seven circuits, the course's own, with what each feeds and its watts: C1 consultation bay, 6 modular, 864 W; C2 uni-sex and female toilets, 5 modular, 720 W; C3 cleaner, male toilets and tea bay, 7 modular, 1008 W; C4 the two stores, 4 twin, 464 W; C5 showroom east, 28 LED, 728 W; C6 service reception, 21 LED, 546 W; C7 foyer, 6 LED and 6 bollards, 264 W. The phases: L1 C1 and C5; L2 C3 and C6; L3 C2, C4 and C7. The rules from screen 6 with their practice values. "(b) Determine the current on L1." A typed answer (part 3b): C1, 864 × 1.25 = 1080 W, 1080 ÷ 220.8 = 4.89 A; C5, 728 ÷ 218.5 = 3.33 A; 4.89 + 3.33 = 8.22 A. Slips: 7.24 A (the ballast left out), 7.87 A (the power factor left out), 10.09 A (the older × 1.8 rule: another method; the question uses the 25% allowance), 24.35 A (the whole board: L1 carries only its own circuits). After it: L2, 5.71 + 2.50 = 8.21 A; L3, 4.08 + 2.63 + 1.21 = 7.92 A; the neutral 0.30 A; lesson 8 sizes DBL2's submain on the heaviest, 8.22 A. After two misses the working ends: part (c) carries the course's 8.22 A. Read: L1 carries 8.22 A. Screen 9, Section A, the course's question 3 (c): 1(a) and 3(b) carried forward (23.08 A, 8.22 A). Given, each practice value labelled: the lighting at 100%, the course's choice, as question 5a has the showroom lights on from 7.30 am to 9 pm: DBL2 8.22 + 8.21 + 7.92 = 24.35 A, and DBL1 38.74 A, worked the same way from its 103 LED, 16 modular, 12 twin and 6 bulkheads (the bulkheads with the LEDs, no ballast allowance), and its 9 wall spots (2 × 35 W)[^44] and 6 columns (70 W)[^45] taken at a power factor of 0.9 (a practice value with no source: the lamps are not named). Sockets: eight 32 A circuits, one per area, each taken at its rating, as standard circuits: 100% of the largest plus 50% of every other. Fixed points: three 20 A DP switches[^46] and a 32 A rotary isolator,[^47] each taken at its rating, as heating and power: 100% of the largest plus 75% of the rest. EV: two charging points of two 32 A outlets[^48][^49] taken as four single-phase outlets (a practice value: the drawing does not say whether the outlets are single- or three-phase), no diversity; the 63 A TPN isolators are not part of the circuit (pack p.5). The motor at 100%, the only one.[^19] The single-phase loads shared evenly, ÷ 3, as an older book works a balanced line current.[^50] "(c) Determine the maximum demand of the installation, per phase." A typed answer (part 3c): 63.09 + 144.00 + 77.00 + 128.00 = 412.09 A; 412.09 ÷ 3 = 137.36 A; 137.36 + 23.08 = 160.44 A (unrounded working gives 160.44 A too; the last place either side is accepted). Slips: 202.78 A (no diversity), 137.36 A (the motor left out), 145.05 A (the motor divided by 3: its Ib is already a line current), 435.17 A (not shared over three phases), 158.34 A (the lighting at 90%: fair as a designer, but the question takes 100%). After it: about 160 A a phase, an estimate on practice values, as question 10 allows; a real split is heavier on one phase: four 32 A EV outlets cannot share evenly over three phases, so one phase carries two, 2 × 32 = 64 A, against an even share of 128 ÷ 3 = 42.67 A, unless other circuits move off it. Read: about 160.44 A a phase. Screen 10, Section B: "State two reasons a designer applies diversity." Your written answer, marked against four points (a full answer makes any two), one more go, then the model answer. Screen 11, Section A, changed numbers: "A small office's single-phase board feeds five 32 A socket circuits, arranged as standard circuits, and lighting with a total current demand of 18.00 A. Using the small shops, stores and offices allowances (standard circuits: 100% of the largest plus 50% of every other; lighting 90%), determine its maximum demand." A typed answer: 32 + 0.5 × 4 × 32 = 96.00 A; 0.9 × 18.00 = 16.20 A; 112.20 A. Slips: 178.00 A (no diversity), 114.00 A (the lighting at 100%), 96.20 A (50% on the largest circuit too). Read: 112.20 A. Screen 12, Keep this: the summary card, then Finish the lesson. The line under the lesson (figures from your slides, your assignment and the drawings; practice values marked; each line worked from the rounded figure before it) shows only on screens 3, 4, 6 to 9 and 11.
interactive.ignores: The bars treat each circuit's current as in step with its own line voltage, as if every fitting had the same power factor; theirs differ a little (0.95 and 0.96 here), which changes the neutral current very little. The circuit currents rest on practice values for ballast loss and power factor, not on the makers' data for the drawing's own fittings. Harmonics are left out: fluorescent and LED fittings can draw third-harmonic currents, which add in the neutral instead of cancelling; that is lesson 4. The bars show steady currents with every fitting on, not switching on, dimming or a lamp failing.

explain.text:
[[Maximum demand]] is the largest current an installation draws at any one time.[^6] It may be worked out for the whole installation or for a part of it,[^7] and it is the current the circuits, switches and protective devices that feed that part normally carry,[^51] so the supply and each submain are chosen for it. It is less than the connected load, because not everything runs flat out together: allowing for that with common sense rather than designing for the maximum is [[diversity]],[^16] and its figures are guidance from the On-Site Guide, not a rule.[^1] On a three-phase board there is a second question as well: which phase each single-phase circuit goes on.

Each lighting circuit runs between one line and the neutral, so its current comes back along the neutral. The three line voltages are a third of a cycle apart, and each circuit's current keeps step with its own line voltage, so the three currents are a third of a cycle apart too; three equal currents spaced like that add up to nothing in the neutral: the balanced three-phase load your slides describe has no neutral current at all.[^13] Make them unequal and they no longer cancel;[^14] what is left over flows in the neutral, so the neutral carries the imbalance, not the total. With the course's practice values for the fittings, put DBL2's seven lighting circuits all on L1, and L1 and the neutral both carry 24.35 A; share them as the course does, and the phases carry 8.22, 8.21 and 7.92 A and the neutral 0.30 A. That is why single-phase circuits are spread about equally across the three phases,[^52] and why the heaviest phase, not the average, sets what the supply must carry.[^15] The picture treats all the fittings as having the same power factor, a simplified case; real fittings differ a little, which moves the neutral current very little.

Diversity takes the total down by type of load. For small shops, stores and offices, for example, the On-Site Guide allows 100% of the largest standard circuit and 50% of every other.[^20] BS 7671 itself has no such table and leaves the assessment to the designer.[^3] Where diversity belongs is argued: your slides apply 66% to one lighting circuit's Ib,[^2] a training provider applies it only to the total at the origin,[^26] and an IET answer says it might only rarely be appropriate for a single circuit's design current.[^27] For EV charge points without load management the IEC wording sets the factor at 1,[^21] which the course follows, though it is argued. Common sense can also say none: the showroom's lights are all on from 7.30 am to 9 pm (your assignment, question 5a), so the course takes them at 100%.

**Maximum demand is the connected load with diversity only where common sense allows, shared across L1, L2 and L3 so that the heaviest phase is as light as it can be.**[^53][^52]

analogy.text: Think of a dockyard canteen. The cooks plan for the busiest sitting, not for everyone on the base eating at once: that is diversity. And they split the diners evenly between three serving counters, decided in advance, so that no one queue sets the pace for the whole room: that is sharing the circuits across L1, L2 and L3.
analogy.breaks: Hungry people can wait; current cannot. If everything does come on together, the installation carries it there and then, which is why a figure with diversity may occasionally be exceeded[^12] and why EV points without load management get none.[^21] And three uneven queues just leave one long one, whereas uneven phase currents also send the difference down the neutral.

practice.text:
- List every load on a schedule of circuits, as your guide asks:[^54] each board's circuits, what they feed and their current.
- Work each load's current from what it really draws: lighting from the key's watts with the ballast loss and power factor from the maker's data (practice values until you have it),[^31][^32] and a motor's Ib as in lesson 1.
- Share the single-phase circuits about equally across L1, L2 and L3[^52] and add up each phase. The heaviest phase sets the size.[^15]
- Apply diversity by type of load where common sense allows, from the On-Site Guide's Appendix A, and write down why. Leave it off where the loads run together, such as the showroom's lighting, and on EV points without load management.[^21]
- Add each three-phase load's line current to every phase, and compare the heaviest phase with the supply.

**Rule of thumb:** when you cannot tell whether loads run together, take them at 100%. Too high a figure costs money; too low a figure leaves the supply and submains carrying more than they were chosen for.

**Worked example:** the showroom (question 10), with the course's practice values. Lighting, 24.35 + 38.74 = 63.09 A. Eight 32 A socket circuits as standard circuits, 32 + 0.5 × 7 × 32 = 144.00 A.[^20] The 32 A and three 20 A points as heating and power, 32 + 0.75 × 3 × 20 = 77.00 A.[^18] Four 32 A EV outlets, 128.00 A. Together 412.09 A, which is 137.36 A a phase when shared evenly; with the motor's 23.08 A on every line, 160.44 A a phase.

**Common mistakes**
- Treating diversity as a rule: it is guidance and need not be applied.[^1]
- Every single-phase circuit on one phase: the neutral then carries the lot.
- Fluorescent tube watts alone: the ballast's loss is extra.[^31]
- Dividing the motor's current by three with the rest: a three-phase load's Ib is already a line current.
- Diversity on EV charge points without load management.[^25]

b1.q: State two reasons a designer applies diversity.

points.text: Not every load runs at full current at the same time, so the real demand is less than the connected load: diversity designs with common sense rather than for the maximum.
The supply, submains and switchgear can be chosen for the demand they will really carry, not for every load at once.
points.cite: Slides p.10 (design using 'common sense' rather than the maximum demand)

b1.model: Not every load runs at full current at the same time, so designing for every load at once overstates what the installation draws; your slides call diversity designing with common sense rather than for the maximum (p.10). Allowing for it keeps cable sizes smaller and costs lower (p.10), and lets the supply, submains and switchgear be chosen for the maximum demand they will really carry. It is guidance from the On-Site Guide, applied with judgement, not a rule.

summary.title: Maximum demand and diversity
summary.for: The largest current the installation, or one board, draws at any one time. The supply and every submain are sized from it; Regulation 311.1 leaves the assessment to the designer.
summary.rule:
Lighting: I = W ÷ (230 × pf), fluorescent tube W × 1.25 first if no ballast loss is given
Neutral, same pf: IN = √(I1² + I2² + I3² − I1·I2 − I2·I3 − I3·I1)
Per phase: single-phase total after diversity ÷ 3, + each three-phase line current

Share single-phase circuits about equally over L1, L2 and L3: the heaviest phase sets the size.
Diversity: On-Site Guide Appendix A, guidance (slides p.10). None on EV points without load management.

Every single-phase circuit on one phase: the neutral carries the lot.
